analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to roughly $15.64 an hour, tied to the poverty line.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or any action after being referred to committee on January 9, 2023, and died with no cosponsors when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act so the minimum wage is recalculated to give a full-time worker an annual income about 25.5% above the federal poverty line for a family of four. The Department of Labor would set that rate — about $15.64 an hour under current poverty thresholds — by June 1, 2023, and update it every four years, with no allowance for downward adjustments. The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and received no further action for the entire two-year Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning at or near the federal minimum wage, who would see their hourly pay more than double from $7.25 to roughly $15.64. The bill also allows states and cities to set higher minimums.

how_it_helps.text: It sets the minimum wage so that a full-time, year-round worker earns at least 25.5% above the federal poverty threshold for a family of four, which the CRS summary estimates at about $15.64 per hour.
The Department of Labor must recalculate the wage every four years and may never lower it, so the floor rises with the cost of living instead of stalling for years as the current $7.25 rate has.
The bill's findings note that a full-time minimum-wage worker earns below the poverty line for a family of four, and that average one-bedroom rent consumes more than 65% of such a worker's income.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum wage — restaurants, retail, hotels, and other low-wage service businesses — would face labor costs more than double the current federal floor, with no gradual phase-in beyond the September 1, 2023 effective date.

drawbacks.text: The jump would be steep and fast: from $7.25 to about $15.64 in a single step taking effect September 1, 2023, with no gradual phase-in schedule or regional adjustment for lower-cost areas.

Small businesses in low-wage sectors such as restaurants and retail would bear the largest cost increase, and some economists argue sharp minimum-wage hikes can accelerate automation or reduce entry-level hiring; supporters counter that the current wage leaves full-time workers in poverty.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and large for the lowest-paid workers, whose pay would more than double under a formula tied to actual living costs. The cost falls on the businesses that employ them, and the single-step, no-phase-in design — versus the graduated schedules in most minimum-wage legislation — would make the transition harder. The bigger obstacle, though, was not design but support: the bill attracted no cosponsors and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Al Green of Texas introduced the bill on January 9, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over the full two-year Congress.
No further action was ever taken: the action history shows only introduction and committee referral, with no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that pay the federal minimum wage are better off, since their wage floor stayed at $7.25. Low-wage workers are worse off, having gained nothing despite the bill's introduction.

for.name: Rep. Al Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 9, 2023, proposing a minimum wage tied to 25.5% above the poverty line for a family of four.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Her committee took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — during the entire 118th Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: 224 House Republicans controlling committee agendas and floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: The bill sat untouched in a Republican-controlled committee, and no minimum-wage increase was brought to the House floor in the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists — but its fate in a Republican-run committee reflected the parties' split on raising the minimum wage.

industries.note: The industry employs the largest share of minimum-wage workers and would face roughly a 115% increase in its wage floor with no phase-in. Keeping the wage at $7.25 means its labor costs stay low while many of its workers remain below the poverty line.

Large low-wage employers in retail, hotels, and care work would pay sharply more per hour. The bill's housing findings note that minimum-wage workers cannot afford average rent, meaning the current floor effectively shifts living costs onto workers and public assistance.
